en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek gives 'selling' no object.

01.r: Rules out a single case of need.
01.n: Abbott-Smith gives this word as a conjunction, 'and not, neither, nor', and also as an adverb; 'not even' gives the adverb's force here.

02.r: Explains the community's state, described in what goes before.

03.r: Lacking what one needs to live.
03.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from ἐνδέω, 'to lack', and gives 'in want, needy'; this verse is its only New Testament use. He notes the Septuagint uses it for Hebrew words including אֶבְיוֹן, needy, poor.

04.r: Any member of the community at all.

05.r: Describes a continuing state of the community.
05.n: An imperfect: over that period, no one was in want.

08.r: Every one of those who owned property, not a chosen few.
08.n: Abbott-Smith: 'how much, how many ... as much as'; here of number, all those who.

09.r: Gives the reason no one was in need.

10.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from κτάομαι, to acquire, and gives 'a possessor'; this verse is its only New Testament use. It is related to κτῆμα, possession.

11.r: Pieces of land, fields or estates.
11.n: Abbott-Smith calls it a diminutive of χώρα, land, with the senses 'a place, region' and 'an estate, property, piece of land'; he puts this verse under the second.

14.n: A fuller verb for 'to be'; Abbott-Smith gives earlier senses 'to begin' and 'to be in existence, be at hand'. An imperfect.

15.r: They sold their land or houses.
15.n: Abbott-Smith gives the first sense as 'to exchange or barter', the second 'to sell'. A present participle beside the imperfect 'were bringing': selling and bringing went on as a practice.

16.r: They kept bringing the money from the sales.
16.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to bear, carry'. An imperfect: a repeated practice, which the BSB's 'would sell ... bring' also shows.

17.r: The particular sums raised by each sale.

18.r: The money received for what was sold.
18.n: Abbott-Smith starts from 'a valuing', and gives first 'a price paid or received', citing this verse for the plural. The same word means honour; in the Septuagint it stands for Hebrew words including עֵרֶךְ, which this study renders 'valuation'.

19.r: The article with the participle that follows: the things being sold.

20.r: The lands and houses as they were sold.
20.n: A different verb for selling from the one earlier in the verse; Abbott-Smith gives it simply as 'to sell'. English has one word for both, so the difference cannot show in the translation. A present passive participle: the things in the course of being sold.

tr_note: Where our text has ἦν, 'was', the Textus Receptus has ὑπῆρχεν, a fuller verb for 'to be'. Both mean 'there was', so the KJV's 'Neither was there' is the same either way.
